chapters.title: Israel is oppressed in Egypt

parts.text: After Joseph and his generation die, the Israelites multiply greatly in Egypt. A new king, who does not know Joseph, fears that they might join Egypt’s enemies. He places them under taskmasters and forces them into harsh labor, building treasure cities and working in brickmaking and the fields. Yet their numbers continue to increase.

Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys, but Shiphrah and Puah fear God and preserve their lives. God deals well with the midwives, and the people continue growing. Pharaoh then commands all his people to throw every Hebrew newborn son into the river while allowing the daughters to live.

chapters.title: Moses is preserved and flees to Midian

parts.text: A Levite mother hides her baby son and later places him in an ark of bulrushes daubed with slime and pitch among the flags by the river. Pharaoh’s daughter finds him and has compassion. Through the child’s sister, his own mother is hired to nurse him. He becomes Pharaoh’s daughter’s son, and she names him Moses.

As an adult, Moses kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew. When the killing becomes known, he flees Pharaoh and settles in Midian. There he protects a priest’s daughters at a well, marries Zipporah, and names their son Gershom. Meanwhile, Israel groans under bondage. God hears their cries and remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

chapters.title: God calls Moses from the burning bush

parts.text: While tending Jethro’s flock near Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed. God calls him, tells him to remove his shoes on holy ground, and identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He has seen Israel’s suffering and sends Moses to bring the people out of Egypt. When Moses questions his fitness, God promises to be with him.

God tells Moses to identify his sender as I AM and as the LORD, the God of their fathers. Moses must gather Israel’s elders and request permission from Pharaoh to worship in the wilderness. God foretells Pharaoh’s resistance, the wonders that will overcome it, and Israel’s departure with Egyptian silver, gold, and clothing.

chapters.title: Signs, objections, and the return to Egypt

parts.text: God gives Moses signs to show Israel: a rod becomes a serpent, his hand becomes leprous and is restored, and river water can become blood. Moses objects that he speaks poorly. God promises to teach him what to say, but when he still asks for someone else, God appoints Aaron as his spokesman.

Moses returns toward Egypt with his family. God calls Israel his firstborn son and warns that Pharaoh’s refusal will bring death upon Pharaoh’s firstborn. During the journey, a dangerous encounter with the LORD ends after Zipporah circumcises her son. Aaron meets Moses, and together they present God’s words and signs to Israel’s elders. The people believe and worship.

chapters.title: Pharaoh increases Israel’s burdens

parts.text: Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh to let Israel hold a feast to the LORD in the wilderness. Pharaoh refuses, denies any obligation to obey the LORD, and accuses the people of idleness. He orders them to gather their own straw while producing the same number of bricks. Their officers are beaten when the daily quota is not met.

The Israelite officers appeal to Pharaoh, but he repeats his demands and dismisses their complaint. Meeting Moses and Aaron afterward, they blame them for making the people hateful to Pharaoh and putting their lives in danger. Moses brings the complaint to the LORD, asking why his mission has brought greater suffering without the promised deliverance.

chapters.title: God renews his promise of deliverance

parts.text: The LORD assures Moses that Pharaoh will eventually drive Israel out. Recalling his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God promises to redeem Israel, take them as his people, and give them the promised land. Their anguish and cruel bondage prevent them from listening. Moses questions how Pharaoh will listen when Israel has not, but God renews the charge to Moses and Aaron.

The chapter records the families of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, tracing the line through Levi to Aaron and Moses and naming Aaron’s descendants. It identifies these brothers as the men commanded to bring Israel out of Egypt. God again tells Moses to speak his words to Pharaoh, while Moses repeats his concern about his speech.

chapters.title: Aaron’s rod and the waters turned to blood

parts.text: God appoints Moses to speak with divine authority before Pharaoh and Aaron to act as his spokesman. He announces that Pharaoh’s hardened resistance will lead to great judgments through which Egypt will know the LORD. Before Pharaoh, Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent. The Egyptian magicians produce serpents too, but Aaron’s rod swallows theirs, and Pharaoh still refuses to listen.

At God’s command, Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh by the river. The waters of Egypt are struck and become blood; fish die, the river stinks, and the Egyptians cannot drink from it. The magicians imitate the sign, and Pharaoh remains unmoved. Egyptians dig around the river for drinking water, and seven days pass after the LORD strikes it.

chapters.title: Frogs, lice, and flies

parts.text: Frogs overrun Egypt after Pharaoh again refuses to release Israel. The magicians also bring up frogs, but Pharaoh asks Moses to pray for their removal and promises to let the people sacrifice. Moses prays, the frogs die, and heaps of them fill the land with a stench. Once relief comes, Pharaoh hardens his heart and breaks his promise.

Dust becomes lice on people and animals. Unable to reproduce this plague, the magicians acknowledge God’s hand, but Pharaoh will not listen. Swarms of flies then afflict Egypt while Goshen is spared. Pharaoh offers limited permission to worship, and Moses insists on going into the wilderness. After Moses prays and the flies disappear, Pharaoh again refuses to release Israel.

chapters.title: Disease, boils, and destructive hail

parts.text: A severe disease strikes Egyptian livestock in the fields, while Israel’s livestock are spared. Pharaoh verifies the distinction but remains hardened. Moses then scatters furnace ashes into the air, and boils break out on people and animals. Even the magicians cannot stand before Moses because of the boils, yet Pharaoh still refuses to listen.

God warns of unprecedented hail and tells people to shelter their servants and animals. Some Egyptians heed the warning. Hail and fire devastate exposed life and crops, but Goshen is untouched. Pharaoh admits his sin and promises release. Moses prays, and the storm stops; nevertheless, Pharaoh and his servants harden their hearts again, and Israel remains in Egypt.

chapters.title: Locusts and darkness

parts.text: Moses warns that locusts will consume what the hail has left. Pharaoh’s servants urge him to yield, but he will permit only the men to go. Moses insists that the whole community and their livestock must worship. Locusts then cover Egypt and devour its remaining greenery. Pharaoh confesses sin and requests prayer; a strong wind removes the locusts, but he still refuses Israel’s departure.

Thick darkness covers Egypt for three days, while Israel has light in its dwellings. Pharaoh now permits the families to leave but demands that their livestock remain. Moses refuses because they will need animals for sacrifice. Pharaoh angrily dismisses him and threatens death if Moses sees his face again.

chapters.title: The final plague is announced

parts.text: The LORD tells Moses that one more plague will cause Pharaoh to release Israel completely. The people are to request silver and gold from their Egyptian neighbors. God gives them favor, and Moses himself is highly regarded among Pharaoh’s servants and the Egyptian people.

Moses announces that the LORD will pass through Egypt about midnight and every firstborn will die, from Pharaoh’s household to the lowest household and among the animals. Egypt will cry out as never before, while Israel will be protected. Pharaoh’s servants will beg the Israelites to leave. Moses departs angrily, but Pharaoh remains hardened despite the wonders already performed.

chapters.title: Passover and the departure from Egypt

parts.text: God establishes the passover. Each household is to kill an unblemished lamb, place its blood on the doorposts, and eat it roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, ready to depart. The blood marks the houses spared when God strikes Egypt’s firstborn. Passover and seven days of unleavened bread are to be remembered in future generations, and parents must explain the deliverance to their children.

At midnight Egypt’s firstborn die. Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron and orders Israel to leave with their families and livestock. The Egyptians urge them out and give them silver, gold, and clothing. About six hundred thousand men depart, besides children, accompanied by a mixed multitude. Israel leaves after the stated 430 years. Further rules define who may share the passover meal, including circumcised strangers.

chapters.title: Remembering deliverance and following God’s guidance

parts.text: The LORD claims Israel’s firstborn, and Moses commands the yearly observance of unleavened bread as a remembrance of deliverance from Egypt. Parents must explain that the LORD brought them out with a strong hand. Firstborn males among clean livestock are set apart for him, while firstborn sons are redeemed; the firstling of an ass must be redeemed with a lamb or have its neck broken.

God leads Israel toward the wilderness and the Red sea rather than the shorter Philistine route, lest war cause them to return to Egypt. Moses carries Joseph’s bones, honoring the oath Joseph required. The LORD goes before the people in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

chapters.title: Israel crosses the sea

parts.text: God directs Israel to camp by the sea, where Pharaoh will think them trapped. Pharaoh regrets releasing them and pursues with chariots and horsemen. Seeing the approaching army, Israel becomes afraid and accuses Moses of bringing them out to die. Moses tells them to stand still, see the LORD’s salvation, and trust him to fight for them.

The cloud moves between Israel and Egypt. At God’s command, Moses stretches out his hand, and a strong east wind divides the sea, making dry ground. Israel crosses between walls of water. The Egyptians follow, but their chariots become disabled. Moses stretches out his hand again, and the returning waters overwhelm the pursuing army. Israel sees the LORD’s power and believes him and Moses.

chapters.title: A song of victory and bitter water made sweet

parts.text: Moses and Israel sing to the LORD for overthrowing Pharaoh’s chariots and army in the sea. They praise his power, holiness, mercy, and deliverance, declaring that no god is like him. The song anticipates fear among surrounding nations and God bringing his people into the place he has prepared. Miriam and the women answer with timbrels and dancing, celebrating the same victory.

After three days without water, Israel reaches Marah, where the water is bitter. The people complain, and Moses cries to the LORD. God shows him a tree that makes the water sweet when cast into it. God calls for obedience and identifies himself as their healer. They then camp at Elim beside twelve wells and seventy palm trees.

chapters.title: Manna, quails, and sabbath rest

parts.text: In the wilderness, Israel complains of hunger and remembers Egypt’s food. The LORD promises meat in the evening and bread each morning, testing whether they will follow his instructions. Quails cover the camp, and a small substance appears with the morning dew. The people call it manna and gather the appointed amount. Some disobey the instruction against keeping it overnight, and it breeds worms and stinks.

On the sixth day they gather twice as much, and the portion kept for the sabbath remains good. No manna appears on the seventh day, despite some people going out to search. God commands sabbath rest. A pot of manna is preserved for future generations, and the chapter records that Israel ate manna for forty years until reaching the inhabited land.

chapters.title: Water from the rock and victory over Amalek

parts.text: At Rephidim, the people lack water and quarrel with Moses, accusing him of bringing them out of Egypt to kill them with thirst. God tells Moses to take the elders and strike the rock at Horeb with his rod. Water comes out for the people. The place is named Massah and Meribah because Israel tested the LORD and questioned whether he was among them.

Amalek attacks Israel. Joshua leads the fighting while Moses stands on a hill with God’s rod. Israel prevails when Moses raises his hand, but Amalek prevails when he lowers it. Aaron and Hur support his weary hands until sunset, and Joshua wins. God commands a written memorial, and Moses builds an altar named JEHOVAH-nissi.

chapters.title: Jethro advises Moses to share the judging

parts.text: Jethro visits Moses in the wilderness, bringing Zipporah and Moses’ two sons. Moses tells him how the LORD rescued Israel from Pharaoh and helped them through their hardships. Jethro rejoices, blesses the LORD, and acknowledges his greatness above all gods. He offers sacrifices, and Aaron and Israel’s elders share a meal with him before God.

Seeing Moses judge the people’s disputes all day, Jethro warns that the burden will exhaust both Moses and the people. He advises Moses to teach God’s laws and appoint trustworthy, God-fearing men who hate dishonest gain to judge ordinary cases. Difficult matters will remain with Moses. Moses follows this advice, appoints rulers over groups of different sizes, and lets Jethro return home.

chapters.title: Israel prepares to meet God at Sinai

parts.text: Israel camps before Mount Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt. God reminds them of their deliverance and promises that, if they obey his voice and keep his covenant, they will be his peculiar treasure, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation. The people agree. God instructs them to prepare, wash their clothes, and respect boundaries around the mountain.

On the third day, thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, and a loud trumpet accompany the LORD’s descent in fire. The mountain smokes and shakes, and the people tremble. Moses speaks, and God answers him. God again warns against breaking through the boundary to look, commanding Moses to bring Aaron while keeping the people and priests from approaching without permission.

chapters.title: The commandments and the people’s fear

parts.text: God identifies himself as the LORD who delivered Israel from Egypt. He commands them to have no other gods, make no images for worship, honor his name, and keep the sabbath holy. They must honor father and mother, and must not kill, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet what belongs to their neighbor. Sabbath rest recalls God’s six days of creation and seventh-day rest.

Frightened by the thunder, trumpet, and smoking mountain, the people ask Moses to speak for God rather than hear God directly. Moses explains that this encounter is meant to turn them from sin. God forbids gods of silver or gold and gives instructions for simple altars, excluding worked stones and steps that would expose nakedness.

chapters.title: Laws concerning servants, injury, and responsibility

parts.text: God gives judgments governing Hebrew servants, including release after six years and provision for a servant who freely chooses to remain. A daughter sold into service receives protections concerning marriage, food, clothing, and release if these duties are withheld. Laws distinguish intentional killing from unintended death and prescribe severe penalties for striking or cursing parents and for kidnapping.

Further judgments address injuries arising from fights, treatment of servants, harm involving a pregnant woman, and compensation proportionate to injury. A servant permanently injured in an eye or tooth must be freed. Owners are held responsible for dangerous animals when they knowingly fail to restrain them, and rules cover losses caused by uncovered pits and fighting oxen.

chapters.title: Restitution, justice, and care for the vulnerable

parts.text: The laws require restitution for stolen livestock and distinguish circumstances surrounding a burglar’s death. They address damage caused by grazing animals or spreading fire, property entrusted to others, disputed ownership, and borrowed or hired animals. Witnesses, judges, and oaths help determine responsibility where the facts are uncertain. Payment varies with the offense and the offender’s responsibility.

Other commands concern seducing an unmarried woman, witchcraft, bestiality, and sacrifice to other gods. Israel must not oppress strangers, widows, or fatherless children; God hears their cries. Loans to poor Israelites must not carry interest, and a pledged garment must be returned before night. The people must honor God and their rulers, give the firstfruits and firstborn, and maintain the holiness required of them.

chapters.title: Justice, sacred seasons, and the promised journey

parts.text: Israel must reject false reports, bribery, and unjust judgments, neither following a crowd into wrongdoing nor favoring someone because he is poor. They must help even an enemy’s straying or burdened animal and remember the stranger’s experience. The land is to rest in the seventh year, and people and animals each seventh day. Three yearly feasts mark unleavened bread, harvest, and ingathering.

God promises to send an Angel ahead to guard Israel and bring them into the prepared land. They must obey his voice and refuse the gods and practices of its inhabitants. God promises protection, provision, and gradual removal of their enemies, allowing the people to increase before occupying the land. Covenants with the inhabitants and their gods would become a snare.

chapters.title: The covenant is confirmed

parts.text: Moses reports the LORD’s words and judgments, and the people promise obedience. He writes the words, builds an altar with twelve pillars representing Israel’s tribes, and arranges sacrifices. After reading the covenant book, he again receives the people’s agreement and sprinkles them with blood, identifying it as the blood of the covenant the LORD has made with them.

Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders ascend and see the God of Israel, with a pavement like sapphire beneath his feet; they eat and drink without being harmed. God summons Moses higher to receive the stone tablets. Leaving Aaron and Hur available to the people, Moses enters the cloud on Sinai and remains on the mountain forty days and nights.

chapters.title: Offerings and furnishings for God’s sanctuary

parts.text: The LORD invites willing offerings of precious metals, cloth, skins, wood, oil, spices, and stones for a sanctuary where he will dwell among Israel. Everything must follow the pattern shown to Moses. Instructions describe the gold-covered ark, its carrying poles, and the mercy seat with two cherubims. God will speak to Moses from above the mercy seat, between the cherubims.

God also specifies a gold-covered table, its vessels and carrying equipment, with shewbread continually before him. A candlestick of pure beaten gold is to have a central shaft, six branches, almond-shaped ornamentation, and seven lamps. Its tools are also gold. Moses is again told to make these furnishings according to the pattern shown on the mountain.

chapters.title: The tabernacle’s curtains, framework, and veil

parts.text: God describes the tabernacle’s inner linen curtains, woven with blue, purple, scarlet, and cherubims. Loops and golden fastenings join them into one covering. A larger covering of goats’ hair lies over them, joined with brass fastenings, with outer coverings of dyed rams’ skins and badgers’ skins. The instructions specify measurements and how the coverings overlap.

Upright boards of shittim wood, covered with gold, stand in silver sockets and are joined by bars. A veil separates the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark and mercy seat belong. The table and candlestick stand outside the veil on opposite sides. An embroidered entrance curtain hangs on five gold-covered pillars with brass sockets.

chapters.title: The altar, courtyard, and lamp oil

parts.text: God commands a square altar of shittim wood covered with brass, with horns at its corners. Its pots, shovels, basins, fleshhooks, and firepans are also brass. A brass grating, rings, and carrying poles complete the structure. The altar is hollow and must follow the pattern shown to Moses on the mountain.

Linen hangings supported by pillars enclose the tabernacle courtyard. The entrance has a colored embroidered hanging, while the posts, sockets, hooks, and other fittings are assigned their materials and measurements. Israel must supply pure beaten olive oil for the lamp. Aaron and his sons are responsible for tending it before the LORD from evening until morning outside the veil.

chapters.title: Holy garments for Aaron and his sons

parts.text: God appoints Aaron and his sons as priests and directs skilled workers to make holy garments for their service. Aaron’s ephod bears two onyx stones engraved with the tribes’ names. His breastplate holds twelve named stones and contains the Urim and Thummim. These garments carry Israel’s names upon his shoulders and heart as he comes before the LORD.

The blue robe has pomegranates and golden bells around its hem. A gold plate on Aaron’s miter bears the words HOLINESS TO THE LORD, and he bears the iniquity connected with Israel’s holy gifts. Coats, girdles, head coverings, and linen breeches are prescribed for the priests. They must be consecrated and properly clothed when approaching the sanctuary and altar, lest they incur guilt and die.

chapters.title: Consecrating the priests and daily offerings

parts.text: God gives instructions for consecrating Aaron and his sons. They are to be washed, dressed in their priestly garments, and anointed. A bullock and two rams are offered, with prescribed uses of their blood and portions. Blood is applied to the priests’ right ears, thumbs, and great toes, and blood and oil are sprinkled on them and their garments. Portions are waved before the LORD.

The consecration extends over seven days, including sacrifices and the priests’ sacred meal. The altar is purified and sanctified. Two lambs are to be offered daily, morning and evening, with flour, oil, and drink offerings. God promises to meet Israel there, sanctify the sanctuary and priesthood, and dwell among the people whom he brought out of Egypt.

chapters.title: Incense, ransom money, washing, and holy oil

parts.text: God commands a gold-covered incense altar before the veil. Aaron must burn incense morning and evening, and its horns receive yearly atoning blood; unauthorized offerings are forbidden there. When Israel is numbered, each counted man gives half a shekel as a ransom for his life. Rich and poor give the same amount, which supports the sanctuary’s service and serves as a memorial before the LORD.

A brass laver stands between the altar and tabernacle so priests can wash hands and feet before ministering. God gives the ingredients for sacred anointing oil and incense. The oil consecrates the sanctuary, furnishings, and priests. Neither mixture is to be copied for ordinary personal use; those who misuse them are to be cut off from their people.

chapters.title: Skilled workers and the sabbath sign

parts.text: God names Bezaleel and fills him with his Spirit, giving wisdom and skill for metalwork, stone-setting, woodcarving, and other craftsmanship. Aholiab is appointed to work with him, and God gives wisdom to other skilled workers. They are to make the tabernacle, its furnishings, the priestly garments, the anointing oil, and the incense according to everything God has commanded.

The LORD again insists that Israel keep his sabbaths as a sign between himself and them throughout their generations. Six days are for work, but the seventh is holy rest, recalling creation and God’s rest. Sabbath profanation carries severe penalties. When God finishes speaking with Moses on Sinai, he gives him two stone tablets written with the finger of God.

chapters.title: The golden calf and Moses’ intercession

parts.text: While Moses remains on the mountain, the people demand gods to lead them. Aaron makes a golden calf from their earrings, builds an altar, and announces a feast. The people sacrifice, eat, drink, and revel. God tells Moses of their corruption and threatens to destroy them. Moses pleads for Israel, appealing to God’s deliverance and promises to the patriarchs, and the LORD relents from the threatened destruction.

Moses descends, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, and confronts Aaron’s excuses. The Levites answer his call to stand with the LORD, and about three thousand men die. Moses returns to seek forgiveness, even offering to be blotted from God’s book. God holds sinners accountable, directs the journey onward, and sends a plague because of the calf.

chapters.title: Moses asks for God’s presence and glory

parts.text: God commands Israel to continue toward the promised land but says he will not go in their midst lest he consume them because of their stubbornness. The people mourn and remove their ornaments. Moses pitches the tabernacle outside the camp, where those seeking the LORD go. The cloud descends when Moses enters, and God speaks with him as a man speaks with his friend.

Moses asks to know God’s way and insists that God’s presence is what distinguishes Israel from other peoples. God promises his presence and rest. Moses then asks to see his glory. God promises to proclaim his name and goodness but says no man can see his face and live. He will shelter Moses in a rock’s cleft as his glory passes.

chapters.title: The covenant is renewed and Moses’ face shines

parts.text: Moses takes two new stone tablets up Sinai. The LORD proclaims his name, mercy, patience, faithfulness, and justice, declaring both forgiveness and judgment of iniquity. Moses worships and asks God to go with the people and pardon them. God renews his covenant and warns Israel not to make alliances with the land’s inhabitants, worship their gods, or enter marriages that would draw them into idolatry.

Commands concerning unleavened bread, firstborn offerings, sabbath rest, harvest feasts, and sacrifices are repeated. Moses remains with the LORD forty days and nights without food or water, and the covenant words are written on the tablets. When he descends, his face shines, frightening the people. He delivers God’s commands and covers his face with a veil between speaking with them and speaking with the LORD.

chapters.title: Willing offerings and skilled workers

parts.text: Moses gathers Israel and repeats the command to rest on the sabbath, including the prohibition against kindling fire that day. He invites willing gifts for the sanctuary: metals, cloth, skins, wood, oil, spices, and precious stones. Skilled people are called to make the tabernacle, its furnishings and courtyard, and the garments needed for priestly service.

Men and women whose hearts are willing bring their offerings. Skilled women spin the required materials, and the rulers provide stones, spices, and oil. Moses identifies Bezaleel as filled by God with wisdom and craftsmanship, with Aholiab joining him in the work and in teaching others. God equips them for designing, weaving, engraving, and making everything the sanctuary requires.

chapters.title: The people give enough and construction begins

parts.text: Bezaleel, Aholiab, and the skilled workers begin the sanctuary work using the wisdom God has given them. Willing offerings continue arriving every morning. The workers tell Moses that the people are bringing more than the project needs. Moses therefore announces that no further gifts are required, and the people stop bringing them; the supplies are sufficient and more than enough.

The chapter records construction of the tabernacle’s curtains and coverings, following the earlier instructions. Linen curtains with cherubims are joined with golden fastenings, and goats’ hair curtains form another covering. Gold-covered boards, silver sockets, and connecting bars form the structure. Workers also make the veil, its pillars, and the embroidered entrance curtain with the appropriate supporting fittings.

chapters.title: The sanctuary’s furnishings are made

parts.text: Bezaleel makes the ark of shittim wood, covers it with gold, and equips it with rings and carrying poles. The mercy seat and its two cherubims are made of pure gold, with the cherubims facing inward and spreading their wings over it. He also makes the gold-covered table, its carrying equipment, and its gold vessels.

The candlestick is fashioned from beaten gold, with six branches, almond-shaped bowls, ornamental knops, and flowers forming one piece with its shaft. Seven lamps and their tools accompany it. The incense altar is made with its horns, gold covering, rings, and poles. The chapter closes with the preparation of the holy anointing oil and pure incense according to the prescribed craftsmanship.

chapters.title: The courtyard and the accounting of materials

parts.text: The workers make the brass-covered altar of burnt offering and its utensils, grating, rings, and carrying poles. The brass laver and its base are made from the lookingglasses of women assembled at the tabernacle entrance. Linen hangings, supporting pillars, and an embroidered gate form the courtyard, with sockets, hooks, and other fittings as prescribed.

An accounting records the materials used for the tabernacle under Moses’ direction, with Ithamar overseeing the Levites’ work. Bezaleel and Aholiab are identified as the leading craftsmen. The gold comes from offerings; the silver includes the half-shekel contributions of the numbered men and supplies the sockets and fittings. The brass is used for the altar, courtyard sockets, utensils, and pins.

chapters.title: Priestly garments and Moses’ inspection

parts.text: The workers make Aaron’s sacred garments as the LORD commanded. Gold is worked into the colored fabric of the ephod, and engraved stones carry the tribes’ names. The breastplate has twelve stones and is fastened to the ephod. They also make the robe with its bells and pomegranates, the linen garments, and the gold plate inscribed HOLINESS TO THE LORD.

With the work complete, Israel brings the tabernacle and all its equipment to Moses. The inventory includes coverings, structural pieces, the ark, table, candlestick, altars, laver, courtyard, and priestly garments. Moses examines everything and sees that the workers have followed the LORD’s commands. He blesses them for completing the work according to the instructions they received.

chapters.title: The tabernacle is erected and filled with glory

parts.text: The LORD tells Moses to erect the tabernacle on the first day of the first month. He specifies the placement of the ark, veil, table, candlestick, altars, laver, and courtyard. Moses is to anoint the sanctuary and its furnishings, then wash, clothe, and anoint Aaron and his sons for their priestly service. Moses follows these commands.

In the second year after the departure from Egypt, Moses sets up the tabernacle and arranges its furnishings, completing the work. A cloud covers the tent, and the LORD’s glory fills it so that Moses cannot enter. Throughout Israel’s journeys, the people move when the cloud rises and remain when it rests. Cloud by day and fire by night mark God’s presence before them.
